#9107. "If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly"

Architects are increasingly, and existentially, anxious about AI. It can already produce images, generate endless options, manipulate form, draft text, analyse information and take on increasing amounts of technical production. The predictable professional response is to become defensive: to identify the bits of architectural work that machines cannot yet do, protect them, regulate them and insist ever more loudly on the special status of the architect.

This is absolutely the wrong response. Architecture has always had a tendency to retreat when it feels threatened: as its actual control over the production of buildings has diminished, it has clung ever more tightly to authorship, professional territory and the idea that certain activities somehow belong uniquely to architects. AI merely makes the weakness of that position more visible.

If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly. If producing drawings, images, options and information constitutes our entire claim to value, we are defining our value in far too limited terms.

We are still, to an astonishing degree, trained to imagine ourselves as mini Corbusiers

The profession has spent decades confusing the production of architectural artefacts with architectural intelligence, and we have run out of road. We are still, to an astonishing degree, trained to imagine ourselves as mini Corbusiers. If we design a back extension, give it a sufficiently enigmatic name, photograph it carefully, attach enough rhetoric, we somehow persuade ourselves that we have made Ronchamp.

Architectural culture has encouraged this inflation for decades, in that every modest building becomes a manifesto, every detail becomes a proposition and every project arrives with the expectation that it should reveal something profound about architecture itself.

But the age of the hero is exhausted. The profession no longer has the cultural authority, the economic power or, frankly, the public attention to sustain this fantasy, however enthusiastically we continue to perform it for one another. AI may simply accelerate the reckoning: if machines can generate endless formal novelty and beautiful images, the architect’s claim to importance can’t continue to rest on being the singular creative intelligence who produces the special object.

Click here to read more about the issues facing architecture in our Performance Review series.

The economic model that supported this fantasy is broken too. Architecture remains notoriously poorly paid relative to the length and cost of its education, the responsibility it carries and the hours it routinely demands. Yet architects have tolerated this for decades because the profession offered another form of compensation – the most important thing of all for architects: recognition, via awards, publications, photographs, lectures, the approval of our peers and the possibility that one small project might provide a tiny share of architectural glory.

We have accepted low pay, long hours, insecure employment and unpaid competitions partly because we have been sold the idea that authorship itself is a reward. If the work is meaningful enough, beautiful enough or visible enough, perhaps the sacrifice will somehow be justified.

That bargain has always been dubious, but it now looks increasingly absurd. Most architects will never become Corbusier, however many evenings they work, and most projects will never become Ronchamp, however much rhetoric is wrapped around them. Architectural status – irrelevant to most outside a handful of people in the profession – has nevertheless become a kind of substitute currency, and architecture has been remarkably successful at persuading people to accept less of the real kind in return.

We need to expand what clients understand architectural value to be, and therefore what they are prepared to pay architects to do

AI makes the bargain even harder to sustain. If the production work on which fees have traditionally depended becomes faster and cheaper, defending the same exhausted model will simply drive fees and salaries down further.

The answer cannot be to produce the same things more efficiently for less money. We need to expand what clients understand architectural value to be, and therefore what they are prepared to pay architects to do.

The more interesting response to AI is not to ask how architects protect what they currently do, but what architects might become capable of doing if some of that work no longer defines them.

With this, architectural intelligence becomes most useful where there is no simple answer. The most interesting projects rarely arrive as neatly defined problems awaiting visually arresting solutions. Instead, they involve conflicting needs, uncertain briefs, difficult sites, volatile markets, limited resources, political constraints and people who want different things. They involve other consultants who know things the architect does not, clients who change their minds, communities whose needs cannot be compressed into a consultation report and materials that stubbornly refuse to behave predictably like lines on a drawing.

This mess is the essence of architecture. The most useful architect is not simply the person who generates a solution, they are someone able to enter an unresolved situation, figure out what the problem actually is, connect different forms of knowledge, make spatial judgements and establish enough structure for something useful to emerge via collective endeavour rather than their own brilliance.

This demands a radically different model of authorship, which is less author and more host. That doesn’t mean becoming a passive facilitator, it means knowing how to bring people together, anticipating problems, establish frameworks within which others can work, exercising judgement, knowing when to intervene, and knowing when to shut up and not be the hero.

It also changes what architects might reasonably be paid for. At present, architecture fees are overwhelmingly organised around a relatively linear journey from brief, to concept, to information, to construction and eventually completion, but much of the work that might make architecture genuinely valuable sits awkwardly around the edges of that process.

Understanding a problem before a brief becomes fixed is often unpaid. Working seriously with communities gets compressed into consultation. Engaging directly with materials and makers is treated as secondary to design. Returning after occupation to understand what worked and what failed is rarely properly funded. Helping a building adapt over years barely appears in conventional fee structures at all.

There is an irony here, because for years architects have tried to make themselves more machine-like

But architects should be paid for diagnosis and briefing, for bringing different forms of knowledge together, for testing possibilities at full scale, negotiating spatial conflicts, post-occupancy work, adaptation and long-term stewardship. Practices should be able to maintain relationships with buildings and communities rather than disappearing at practical completion. Architecture fees might begin to pay for judgement over time, rather than simply production on the way towards an object.

This is not some romantic idea of architects becoming artists, activists or community workers instead of running viable businesses (which contemporary practice is not). Quite the opposite: it is about identifying forms of architectural value that are difficult to automate and, more importantly, are actually useful.

For the past 20 years, our educational initiative Studio in the Woods (pictured top and left) has accidentally provided a small laboratory for some of this. Its significance has never really been the timber structures that emerge over several days of co-production. Instead, the interesting aspect of Studio in the Woods is what happens when people design and make together under conditions in which the answer is not known beforehand, where ideas encounter the friction of weight, resistance, gravity, tools and materials. Where experts and non-experts work together as equals, and leadership moves according to what needs to happen next.

The skill of the architect in these situations is not to surrender judgement, but to exercise it differently. What should be negotiated? What can remain unresolved? Where is precision necessary? Where might uncertainty be productive? Who knows something that I do not? These are much more interesting questions for the future of the profession than whether AI can draw a convincing building.

There is an irony here, because for years architects have tried to make themselves more machine-like: eliminating uncertainty, standardising processes, increasing predictability, producing ever-more information and pretending that buildings can be completely resolved before anybody actually makes them. Now, machines are becoming extremely capable at exactly those things and we are surprised to find ourselves threatened, and we should stop trying to beat them at their own game.

Human architectural intelligence is at its richest when it is situated, relational and embodied. It involves judgement without complete information and responsibility for consequences that cannot be fully predicted. It means understanding materials as part of landscapes and economies, buildings as things that change through occupation, and design as something produced between many people rather than delivered by one.

None of this means drawings, technical knowledge, form or aesthetic judgement cease to matter. They matter enormously, but they are merely parts of architectural intelligence, not its definition.

The architect of the future does not need to be the person with the most original idea and the most charisma. They might instead be the person who can understand an uncertain situation, recognise what matters, establish a framework for action and create the conditions in which something richer than their own initial idea can emerge. AI may make the old version of the architect less necessary, but I’m not sure that is something we should mourn.

Piers Taylor is the founder of architecture practice Invisible Studio and the convenor of Studio in the Woods. He is professor of knowledge exchange in architecture at the University of the West of England and an external examiner at the Arts University Bournemouth, having previously held positions with the Architectural Association and the University of Cambridge. He holds a PhD from the University of Reading. He has presented several architecture shows on television including BBC programmes The House that £100k Built and The World’s Most Extraordinary Homes. His first book, Learning from the Local, was published in 2025.

As they lift our gaze from our phones, we'll start looking up.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Did you ever see the 2021 Leonardo DiCaprio film Don't Look Up? I don't think it's a spoiler to say that its focus on people not looking up was partly a satire on climate change denial. But more broadly, it fed into the idea that nowadays, we're all looking down a lot; specifically at our phones.

I've honestly got no idea if smart glasses – some of which can now project information, images and videos straight at your eyeballs – will end up taking off in future, and replacing the smartphone. But if they do, then it occurs to me that this will be big news for billboards.

You might assume that if more digital tech catches on, physical advertising would be one of the casualties. After all, why look at a poster when your glasses can show you something tailored? But the more I think about it, the more convinced I am the opposite will happen.

Consider this: nobody is going to wear smart glasses to look at their feet. The whole attraction is that you get the benefits of a phone while keeping your eyes on the world around you. And in most towns and cities – even in this smartphone era – that world is already plastered with outdoor advertising.

And if smart glasses can truly take advantage of augmented reality – tech that overlays digital content onto real-world, physical things – then those billboards will suddenly be a lot more exciting to look at.

For over a century, billboards have been essentially a one-way medium. QR codes promised to fix that, but how many of us have actually stopped in the street, taken out our phones and waggled them at a pixelated square? Once or twice, maybe. But on a regular basis? Hardly.

In future, I reckon, you'll be able to point smart glasses at a billboard and get it to do all sorts of useful things, probably by talking to an AI bot embedded in your specs.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

With a movie billboard, for instance, you might want to play the trailer or find out which cinema it's playing at nearby, and when. You might even want turn-by-turn directions to the multiplex to appear in front of your very eyes.

This might sound like Black Mirror-style sci-fi, but it's worth remembering how many old Black Mirror episodes have essentially come true already. And it certainly seems to be the way the ad industry is thinking.

In fact, you can already see a version of this idea in east London. Electric Garden, on Shoreditch High Street, bills itself as “the billboard you can walk into”. It’s a 21,000 sq ft open-air site that sits behind a row of giant digital screens, so brands can run a campaign on the screens and then build a physical world behind them for people to explore.

Its launch campaign, for Activision’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, turned the site into a neon-lit, Seoul-inspired alleyway, complete with convenience stores, plastic stools and code-breaking missions. As co-founder Alex Ezen puts it: “A screen can capture attention, but a physical experience gives people a reason to stop, take part and share it.”

Smart glasses could deliver something similar without anyone needing to build an alleyway. That will make the brief for designers all the harder, of course, but personally, that’s the kind of challenge I’d relish.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. #9105. Installation Featuring Names of Children Killed in Gaza Refused Display by Local Australian Council

Phil Buehler’s Wall of Tears installation, featuring the names of 18,457 children killed in Gaza between October 7, 2023, and July 19, 2025, has been refused display by a local council in the Australian state of New South Wales, reports the Guardian. The installation was meant to be exhibited at the Shoalhaven Regional Gallery in Nowra on Tuesday and was organized by Shoalhaven Friends of Palestine.

The council told the organizers to look into hiring “armed guards” in case “community conflict” arises. “We were like, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me,’ but we still wrote back to them and said we would meet all the requirements you want. We didn’t even know where we could get armed guards, or if you could get them,” said Annette Pham, a member of the group, adding that they were advised not to advertise the event and were told to reduce the exhibition’s run from eight days to three. Related Articles French Court Faults Deauville City for Removing AP Photograph of Gaza from Exhibition Children's YouTube Star Ms. Rachel to Present Gaza Art Exhibition and Fundraiser

In an email correspondence, it shows New South Wales chief executive Andrew Constance opposing the event and citing staff safety concerns. Pham wrote to the council saying that the “very suggestion that armed guards might be necessary for an exhibition commemorating dead children is deeply disturbing. We are organizing a memorial art exhibition, not an event for which Council has disclosed any specific credible threat of violence requiring consideration of armed protection and metal screening.”

In response, a council spokesperson issued a statement saying that “the installation was deemed to present an unacceptable level of risk to gallery staff, visitors and tenants of the building.”

Buehler’s mural was exhibited in September in front of Parliament House in Canberra, the country’s capital city. The installation was first publicly shown in New York on January 29, coinciding with the second anniversary of the death of Hind Rajab.

Instead, Buehler’s installation will now be shown at the Berry Uniting Church, beginning Thursday. “If people would just look at that, how can that be dangerous? The danger is put on by other people who are trying to turn it into something it’s not,” said Buehler, whose artwork has toured Adelaide and Perth in Australia.

#9104. Minimalist House in Japan by FORM/Kouichi Kimura is "reduced to the essentials"

A monochrome palette and pared-back, open interiors define the aptly named Minimalist House, a home in Japan designed by local studio FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects.

Located in Shiga prefecture, the 73-square-metre home is formed of cubic volumes clad in corrugated metal and black render, perched on a hill overlooking the nearby Lake Biwa.

Minimalist House was designed for a single occupant, but FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects wanted to challenge the assumption that this would mean small-feeling interiors.

This led the studio to create a series of voids and long sightlines that it said help to “liberate space”.

“When hearing ‘a home for a single occupant’, people typically imagine a compact house,” founder Kouichi Kimura told Dezeen.

“Here, living alone is regarded not as a spatial constraint, but as a condition that liberates space,” he added.

“Starting from the individual as the base unit, the house explores a new way of single-person living through the minimal composition reduced to the essentials, with the space that invites in the surrounding view, light, wind, and sound.”

The plan of Minimalist House revolves around a tall void cut through its centre, which extends upwards into a skinny, double-height volume projecting from its roof with a large window.

Finished with grey-plastered walls and dark stone floors, a kitchen, dining space and study occupy the ground floor, with metal and concrete steps leading up to a living space and bedroom above.

Facing the road, the front of the home has been left almost entirely blank. Instead, the interiors open up on the opposite side towards views of the lake in the distance, with the dining table, study and bed pushed up against large, deep-set windows.

“Each floor is designed as a single open layout,” explained Kimura. “The double-height space vertically connects the upper and lower levels. Manipulating floor and ceiling levels gently articulates each space without clearly dividing them.”

“The living space on the upper level is designed not only for daily life, but also for enjoying music. Within the double-height volume, sound resonates off the walls and ceiling, filling the entire space,” he added.

A glass corridor with sliding doors separates the main home from a single-storey washroom, which the studio introduced to ensure that this everyday passage would capture views out over the lake.

“Placing these wet areas away from the main structure creates a natural flow of movement in daily life,” Kimura explained.

“Walking through the glazed corridor in between allows one to touch the landscape, light, and breeze, offering a gentle transition in the everyday time,” he added.

Minimalist forms and interiors often feature in the work of FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects, with the studio’s previous projects in Shiga including a blocky hair salon and home and a skinny home with carefully-placed windows to avoid overlooking.

#9103. The story behind Grant Wood’s American Gothic and what made it go viral

Grant Wood’s sister Nan Wood Graham and his dentist Byron McKeeby were the models for American Gothic (1930) Photo: rarehistoricalphotos.com. Painting: © 2026 Figge Art Museum, successors to the Estate of Nan Wood Graham/Licensed by VAGA at ARS, NY

Grant Wood’s painting American Gothic (1930)—the realist depiction of an austere rural man and woman posed stiffly before a modest white house with a gothic-styled window—has seeped into the public consciousness on a par with Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa and Edvard Munch’s The Scream. “I never stopped watching the ways American Gothic has transitioned into the iconic ‘couple with the pitchfork’ over the past six decades,” says the US art historian Wanda Corn, whose new book The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon delves into the cultural history of the painting.

Over the decades, Corn says she accumulated an “immense archive of reimagined couples” and her publication “sheds critical light on the cultural forces that transformed an image with humble roots into a global icon whose reach and charisma extend far beyond the world of art”, according to the publisher, Princeton University Press.

Corn, professor emerita of art history at Stanford University, outlines in detail how Wood picked his sitters: his 30-year-old sister, Nan Wood Graham, and his 62-year-old dentist, Byron McKeeby. “The two men shared a sense of humour, often chuckling over their ‘bridge for a bridge’ exchange; the dentist had provided the artist with a dental bridge and Wood paid him with a painting of a Paris bridge,” Corn writes.

Crucially the image has been misconstrued over the decades, with viewers interpreting the couple as married when in reality the pair represented a father and his daughter, according to the artist’s sister. “In Wood’s mind, the two people in front of the house represented a father and his aging daughter—a spinster—living in small-town America,” writes Corn. Wood and his closed circle described it this way repeatedly, she adds.

“Yet when the painting went out into the world, not one person saw the couple as a parent and child, nor did they see them as from a small town … this is one of the best examples in the history of art of how an artist’s intentions in a work can differ from the public’s reception of a painting.”

The person who corrected Corn about this widespread misconception was Wood Graham herself. “I too thought it represented a married couple,” Corn says. She explains that when she was photographed as the pitchfork couple with her husband in the 1970s, for a feminist work called Joe and Wanda Corn, Holiday Card (1975) by Keith M. Jones Sr, she was “under the assumption that [Wood’s sitters] were a married couple. But when I went to see [Wood Graham], I talked about them as a couple and she said in no uncertain terms: ‘They’re not a couple. It’s a father and daughter.’”

The image, and Wood’s achievements as an Iowa-based artist, were consistently lambasted and dismissed though. Early art historical texts initially ignored him, such as A History of Art (1962) by H.W. Janson, which only included the work in its seventh edition published in 2006. Corn’s survey of such texts establishes, she says, “how passive-aggressive the coverage of American Gothic was in this literature”.

Wanda Corn, the author of the new book, with her husband Joe Corn in 2024 Photo: Keith M. Jones, Jr.

The critical reaction to a Wood show Corn curated in 1983 was also brutal. “A writer of a Wall Street Journal article in May 1983 … labelled it the ‘Great Grant Wood Redemption Campaign’ and quoted the reaction of a well-known art dealer in town: ‘Flush it down the drain. It’s just cornball, provincial, nationalistic propaganda and it has nothing to do with art!’”

Corn’s 1983 exhibition of Wood’s work, Grant Wood: The Regionalist Vision, which launched at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York, toured to other venues such as the Minneapolis Institute of Art (Yale University Press published an accompanying book). “The last landing of the exhibition was in San Francisco [at the de Young museum], and what better place to launch the first gay Gothic [work] on the walls of a major museum than in San Francisco,” she says, referring to the 1983 front cover of the gay magazine Frontiers that was included in the show.

The author unpicks the thorny issue of Wood’s sexuality, which has come under the microscope in recent years. “The upshot is that Wood today is seen as a far more complicated and tragic figure than he presented and for many years was understood to be,” she writes, acknowledging that two art historians, Tripp Evans and Sue Taylor, have contributed the most to recent psychosexual interpretations of Wood’s life and “the uncovering of his homosexuality”.

“I can see his struggles constantly,” Corn says. “But on the other hand, I also know people who found him just boundless fun to be with, lovable and endlessly creative, not dark and gloomy … we have to get a more balanced view [of him].”

How American Gothic came to be assimilated into the art history canon, across high and low popular culture is also explored through a wide variety of images including Obama Gothic (2012) by Mario Piperni, which shows Michelle and Barack Obama in front of the White House as the pitchfork couple, and Barry Kite’s photocollage Gothic Wave (2010) that draws on Hokusai’s famous 19th-century woodblock print.

“I actually could not have written the book I wrote now back then [in 1983] because I didn’t have the raw data,” Corn says. “I didn’t have this notion of the episodic uses of [the image] for everyday transient events and political events. I didn’t have any sense of what the computer was going to do to the image: the way it was going to translate it but also just make it a resource anybody could tap into.”

• Wanda Corn, The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon, Princeton University Press, 312pp, $49.95/£42 (hb)

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you plan to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as quickly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

Side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

One of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Company). Here is the honest comparison.

A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

An LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

Self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage (67 cents per mile), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $72,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

The biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

The 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

Batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

The FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice says to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

But here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

The decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the important thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

Pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

Pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

Your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

Once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

Pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

The most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Check your employment contract and company handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

Most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

Businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $72,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

Dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP quickly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.

#9100. France Opens War Crimes Investigation into Israeli Bombing of Beirut that Killed Artist Ali Cherri’s Parents

In an apparent legal first, the French War Crimes Unit has opened an investigation into the 2024 Israeli bombing of a Beirut residential building where the family of French Lebanese filmmaker and artist Ali Cherri lived. The announcement comes six months after Cherri and the Paris-based International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) filed a complaint alleging that the Israeli military intentionally targeted a civilian structure, killing seven people, including the artist’s parents, which amounted to a war crime.

The complaint centers on the Israeli military’s bombing of a residential building in Beirut’s Noueiri neighborhood, just hours before a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hezbollah was set to take effect. The strike destroyed the ninth-floor apartment home to the artist’s parents, Mahmoud Naim Cherri and Nadira Hayek, as well as Birki Negesa, a domestic worker employed by the couple. The building’s seventh and eighth floors were also destroyed. Related Articles Israel Returns 22 Looted Antiquities to Greece Billionaire Igor Tulchinsky, Who Sponsored the Bayeux Tapestry's UK Sojourn, Also Funded a Mental Health Facility in an Illegal West Bank Settlement

“To our knowledge, this is the very first judicial investigation opened into the crimes committed by the Israeli army in Lebanon since October 2023,” said Clémence Bectarte, lawyer and coordinator of the FIDH Litigation Action Group. “We hope that this investigation will shed full light on the bombing of 26 November 2024, which we qualified as a war crime in our complaint.”

Cherri, who lives and works between Paris and Beirut, is one of Lebanon’s most prominent contemporary artists. He received the Silver Lion at the 2022 Venice Biennale, where he showed his sculpture triad Titans and video installation Of Men and Gods and Mud (both 2022) in the main exhibition, “The Milk of Dreams,” curated by Cecilia Alemani. His recent exhibition at Almine Rech in New York, “Last Watch Before Dawn,” continued a longstanding preoccupation of his practice: the archaeology of conflict and its excavation in the mind and political memory.

As Cherri holds dual French and Lebanese nationality, the judicial investigation will focus only on the bombing of the apartment. According to the FIDH, the French courts do not have jurisdiction over the events that led to the deaths of the victims, who were not French nationals.

“The opening of this judicial investigation marks another important step in our fight against impunity and our struggle for justice for those who were killed. For my family and me, it is essential that this investigation establish responsibility, and ensure that those who ordered and carried out this bombing are held accountable for their actions,” Cherri said in a statement.

Israel launched a military campaign in Lebanon in September 2024, saying it aimed to target the Iran-allied militant group Hezbollah. The campaign involved aerial bombardments across the Beirut region and a ground invasion of southern Lebanon, displacing roughly 1 million people. In April, the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) reported that Israeli forces had committed nearly 10,000 violations of the ceasefire agreement in less than a year, including more than 500 airstrikes in Lebanon, carried out on an “almost daily” basis. The UN also warned of a “mounting toll of civilian deaths and injuries.”

Israel has consistently rejected accusations that it has violated the ceasefire, characterizing its actions in southern Lebanon as responses to what it describes as violations by Hezbollah.

Recently, I’ve written for Creative Bloq's sister site Digital Camera World about a run of photographic rediscoveries. For instance, F Holland Day’s 1898 series The Seven Words resurfaced in September. Then in October, we saw a newly found cache of photos that document the making of the 1926 horror film Faust. These antiquated forms of physical media sat untouched for a century or more, and yet remain totally viewable. Amazing, really.

Now, let's do a thought experiment. If you're old enough, picture the digital work you made 20 years ago. That might be a website design, assets for a CD-ROM, a vector illustration… whatever.

Ask yourself: could you locate and open those files today? If you’re anything like me, the honest answer is “mostly no”.

It's ironic, really. Because digital work has no tangible physical presence, we tend to think of it as eternal. In truth, though, it's kind of the opposite.

This March, I visited memory card manufacturer Lexar’s facilities in Shenzhen, China. And one moment there has stuck with me ever since.

In a press conference, the company's representative explained that the flash memory used in consumer memory cards and SSDs can start losing data within a year if you leave them in a drawer and don't power them up.

Lexar told me it’s developing a dedicated device to address this issue, but it's early days. In contrast, a print just sits there, being a print.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Meanwhile, if you're putting your work online, there's more bad news. A Pew Research Center study found that 38% of webpages that existed in 2013 were no longer accessible a decade later. Platforms are no safer. Back in 2019, MySpace admitted that a server migration had wiped photos, videos and music uploaded between 2003 and 2015: an estimated 50 million songs from 14 million artists.

Its advice to users was to keep their own backups. But wherever you back stuff up, basically, you're running the same risk. As the sudden closure of Sora highlighted, venture capitalists don't really care about protecting your stuff as much as you do.

There's also the problem of actually opening files in years to come. Built something in Flash in 2012? I doubt you'll be able to salvage it now, after Adobe shuttered the format in 2020, and that's just one example among many.

So what can we do? There are few basic rules we all should be following if we want to be able to access our work in 2030, 2040 and further ahead. The first is to follow the 3-2-1 rule. Keep three copies of anything important, on two different types of storage, with one stored offsite or in the cloud. It's not a foolproof method, but it does reduce the odds of losing stuff exponentially.

Secondly, every few months or so, power up your SSDs and memory cards, so firmware can do its job. Thirdly, export your final files to open formats like TIFF, PNG, SVG or PDF/A, which are more likely to be readable in decades to come.

Fourthly, treat platforms as shop windows, not storerooms. And finally, print your work. As long as you can avoid floods or fires, paper-based storage has a better track record than digital.

Is this seems a bit of a faff, I'd have to agree. But consider this. If future historians end up knowing more about 1926 than 2026, it won’t be for lack of material. It’ll be because we couldn't be bothered to look after it – and what will future generations think of us then?

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. #9098. Chinese Artist Sun Xun’s ‘Magic Atlas’ Is First Animated Feature in Tokyo International Film Fest Competition

Chinese artist and filmmaker Sun Xun never expected “Magic Atlas” to become the first animated feature selected for the Tokyo International Film Festival’s competition.

“I never thought of ‘Magic Atlas’ as an animated film. To me, it brings together many art forms. Animation is simply the label we use for its form. I’m glad people at TIFF understood the effort I put into it,” Sun tells Variety.

“Magic Atlas,” a decade in the making, is set in Luocha, a coal-mining empire where flying is forbidden. Every 60 years, a festival leaves the population unable to remember the era that came before. After a magician is arrested, he meets an orphan boy in prison and gives him the Magic Atlas. The book points the boy toward a past the empire has tried to erase.The film moves between woodblock prints, ink painting and vivid color. Its images often do the work that a conventional plot might spell out, drawing on art and visual traditions from different periods and cultures. Related Articles Sun Xun at Sean Kelly A New Generation of Chinese Artists

Sun says the film was shaped by global events, including the pandemic and the war in Ukraine, as well as personal changes such as his conversion to Buddhism. He put all his savings into the project. When galleries shut down during the pandemic, his art sales dried up. He says he had to find buyers himself and take out loans to keep the film going.

“In my own artistic thinking, I believe every creator should have one ‘all-in’ moment in their life: to make a defining work that takes everything out of them. For me, ‘Magic Atlas’ was that all-in moment,” he says. “I hoped to finish it before my child grew up and while my parents were still alive. Sadly, my father passed away a year before the film was completed.”

Rather than comment on any one event, Sun says, he drew on different cultural and political influences to reflect the divisions he sees around the world. He also brought in images of ancient civilizations, including the pyramids, alongside mythological elements.

“Film cannot address reality directly, but it can take a wider view. It can express how we understand the world and what we are curious about,” he says.

Asked whether films need to explain their stories clearly, Sun says: “I’m actually against ‘story.’ I don’t mean that films shouldn’t have stories. I object to films that emphasize story for the sake of packaging and commercial purposes. As an art form, film should express a state of being.”

Sun names Andrei Tarkovsky, citing 1983’s “Nostalghia,” and the late Hungarian filmmaker Béla Tarr as filmmakers he admires. “They are sincere in the way they approach existence. They don’t rely only on imagined narratives. To me, that is the kind of artistic form cinema should have,” he says.

While working on “Magic Atlas,” Sun studied Dunhuang murals, Song dynasty painting and calligraphy, along with imagery from other cultures. Asked if he worries that some viewers might find the film difficult to follow, he says: “There will always be a barrier to entry. Ten years of work naturally gives the film depth. But I made this important work for myself. My goal was to realize it, not to please every viewer.”Sun says exhibitions connected to “Magic Atlas” are planned in the U.S. and Singapore, though venues and dates have not been unveiled. He has also begun a new feature he calls “All or Nothing,” whose Mandarin title, “Fuyou,” means “Mayfly.” The film will continue the world of “Magic Atlas,” moving from the broad theme of forgetting to an individual experience of memory loss. Sun says he filmed the first shot at an exhibition space in Hangzhou and hopes to finish the feature within two years.

Master plan designs for the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity museum in California have been released, showing galleries connected via a bridge in an adapted 1960s warehouse and a landscape designed by Field Operations.

The updated design for the property in Novato, California, includes the 400-foot-long Great Hall, which the studios said will be “one of the largest single-span spaces for art installations in the country”, a 275-seat theatre, a Japanese-inspired garden and children’s play spaces.

The Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity (the Eames Institute) bought the 88.5-acre property in 2025 to establish a public exhibition space and museum for its collection of furniture and other objects designed by architects Charles and Ray Eames.

The site includes a sawtooth-roofed warehouse and office building designed by architects Jan Lubicz-Nycz and John Savage Bolles, which were originally built for the McGraw-Hill publishing company in 1965.

Shoe company Birkenstock USA operated out of the site until 2019. The Eames Institute now plans to adapt the landscape and buildings for the project.

Architecture studios Herzog & de Meuron and EHDD were signed onto the project when it was first announced last year, and with this most recent update, Field Operations has been announced as the landscape designer.

“What makes this place so extraordinary is the relationship between its remarkable architecture and the landscape of Marin County,” said Field Operations partner Richard Kennedy.

“We imagined the grounds as a living extension of the museum. The idea is simple: ten landscapes, hundreds of places, and infinite journeys.”

According to the team, the warehouse will contain galleries, maker spaces, a theatre and a cafe, while the former office building will be converted into a pavilion for events.

Visitors will enter the warehouse building past a fountain, into a “warm, wood-clad space” containing admissions and the museum shop.

A grand stair will lead to a 120-foot polished stainless-steel bridge that traverses the gallery spaces below. The renders show the spaces as largely open-plan, with the enormous concrete bevels of the roof exposed above.

Other spaces, such as wood and ceramic workshops, will be distributed throughout the building. According to the team, the material palette will primarily consist of colour-stained plywood and plaster, and aluminium windows to “create a dialogue between old and new”.

For the landscape, Field Operations looked to an original plan by landscape architect Tito Patri, which used berms to help bury the buildings into their surroundings, buffering them from a highway which runs directly in front of the site.

The design includes a reconfigured parking and arrival sequence, gardens to the north and south of the warehouse, native stormwater gardens and custom furniture designed by the studio.

Overall, the masterplan will “transform what was once a private, truck-oriented industrial campus into a public cultural destination”, according to the team.

“For my grandparents, design was always grounded in curiosity and intention – looking closely, asking questions, embracing constraints, and finding beauty in the practical and the functional,” said Eames Institute co-founder Llisa Demetrios.

“The museum carries that spirit forward, and it feels especially meaningful to do so in a building that asked us to do the same: work within a remarkable existing structure to imagine what else it can become,” she continued.

Groundbreaking is expected for 2028, with openings projected to begin in 2030.

The project has garnered some criticism for being backed by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, who was appointed America’s first Chief Design Officer in 2025 under President Donald Trump.

Dezeen spoke to Gebbia about the appointment in 2025.

The Eames Institute was founded in 2023 and opened a California headquarters in 2024. San Francisco-based design agency Manual created its current brand identity and logo around the same time.

From the first ever touchscreen on Mac to the super bright and colourful 'PROLED' XDR display, there are quite a few candidates for the headline feature of Apple's new MacBook Pro. But judging by the reaction in the room during the launch in LA last week, the most popular addition might not be that new at all.

Readers of a certain vintage will remember the illuminated Apple logo. The light-up fruit used to adorn every Apple laptop, and was a (somewhat distracting) mainstay of cafes, trains and DJ performances. In 2015, Apple unceremoniously killed the illuminated logo, replacing it with a mirrored version. But as of last week, it's back – and it seems people are happy about it.

Now, the cynical among you might think the reason for the addition is to make the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display stand out as new in public. There's always something to differentiate a new Apple product from the previous generation, even if it's simply new colours. But from a distance, this new MacBook Pro looks almost identical to non PROLED models. How are we supposed to quietly show it off in a cafe? With the 'new' illuminated logo, of course!

But the less cynical among you might see this as yet another sign that under new CEO John Ternus, Apple is rediscovering its sense of fun. From the brand's wild new TikTok presence to the colourful (and cheap) MacBook Neo, Apple seems to be stepping outside of its space grey prison and embracing a sense of friendliness we haven't seen for years. And it's going down well.

#9095. Why Mary Cassatt was more than just a painter of the 'modern Madonna'

Mary Cassatt's The Boating Party (1893-94) National Gallery of Art, Chester Dale Collection

As the centennial of the death of Mary Cassatt (1844-1926) brings renewed attention to the US-born Impressionist, a new publication challenges the image of her as a sentimental painter of mothers and daughters. In Cassatt Reconsidered, Mary G. Morton uses her expertise as a curator and head of French paintings at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, to examine how the art world shaped Cassatt’s reputation, and posits a broader view of her within radical French Modernism.

The book coincides with major exhibitions on Cassatt, including at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris (until 31 January 2027), the Art Institute of Chicago (until 3 January 2027) and the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut (7 November-14 February 2027). Looking closely at the artist’s work and framing her within the experience of women in a modern Paris, Morton shows why Cassatt deserves another look.

The Art Newspaper: What prompted your reassessment?

Mary G. Morton: I thought I knew enough about Cassatt until a 2014 exhibition at the National Gallery on Cassatt’s artistic pas de deux with Degas emphasising their radical technical experimentation. A few years later, an encounter with the PhD candidate Nicole Georgopulos transformed Woman with Sunflower (1905) in my mind from a generic mother and child image to a complex realist allegory, a kind of feminist manifesto responding to and supporting the contemporary suffrage movement. The public recognises Cassatt’s name but associates her with images of maternity. There is so much more to her art, to her story.

How did the art market contribute to the narrowing of Cassatt’s reputation?

Her dealer essentially marketed her as a painter of motherhood, the painter of the “modern Madonna”, hiring critics to write about her in this vein. And while he had success selling her work, the strategy did not serve her well in art historiography. Another dynamic is the burgeoning field of American art history in the 20th century, when Cassatt became an asset to curators as an Impressionist. In most major US museums, her work hangs with US artists, depriving her of the aesthetic context in radical French Modernism. She looks loud, garish, awkward, whereas if you put her with Degas, Renoir and Morisot, she fits in.

Cassatt's Woman with a Sunflower (around 1905) National Gallery of Art, Chester Dale Collection

What would you like museums, scholars and the public to see differently about Cassatt?

It would be great if Cassatt could exit the limited box she has been put into. Cassatt was the most successful avant-garde artist of the 19th century to represent the lived experience of women in modern urban Paris. She created a fresh visual vocabulary for women’s interests and concerns, refusing the oppressive social norms of her class and producing an extraordinary body of work. Cassatt brings us women’s side of the story.

The primary aim of this book is to provoke readers who might be familiar with Cassatt as a misty-eyed painter of mothers and children to look again. My hope is that the book compels people into museums to find Cassatt’s art and experience what I have: brilliantly expressive, innovative objects that relay a unique vision of humanity and of women’s lives as they were lived more than 100 years ago.

• Mary G. Morton, Cassatt Reconsidered, Getty Publications, 208pp, $35 (hb)

#9094. Henry Holland creates wallpaper and fabric collection with a "language developed through ceramics"

Designer Henry Holland‘s textual fabric and textile collection for luxury interior furnishings company Harlequin was informed by his work as a ceramicist, he tells Dezeen in this interview.

Simply named Harlequin x Henry Holland, the collection of wallpapers and fabrics was heavily influenced by both the extensive archive of Harlequin’s parent company Sanderson and Holland’s love of the Japanese pottery technique nerikomi.

“The starting point for the collection was our ceramic work,” Holland told Dezeen. “We used the organic patterns and forms created in our handbuilt work as the starting point, and then similarly we built the colour palettes around the clays that we use to create our pieces.”

“To add further depth and range to the collection, we also delved into the incredibly rich archive that the Sanderson group have across all of their brands and reinterpreted some archive prints that felt like the right additions to the collection.”

The collection features four distinct fabrics that translate ceramic patterns and colours into materials that can transform interior spaces.

For Holland, this transformation of scale, from a hand-held object to entire rooms and interiors, was the most exciting part of the collaboration.

“For me, the collection is really about taking the language we have developed through ceramics and allowing it to live on a completely different scale,” he said.

“At the studio we make objects that sit within a room, whereas with Harlequin we suddenly had the opportunity to take those patterns, colours and textures and make them become the room,” he added.

“There is something really exciting about that shift in perspective. Our work has always been about balancing the graphic with the organic, and I think that really comes through in the collection. There are moments that feel bold and energetic and others that are much softer and quieter.”

Holland worked closely with the Harlequin team to understand which elements of the nerikomi technique could be translated and upscaled to fabric. He found clear similarities in methodology between the technique and the process of making textile fabrics.

“With nerikomi, the pattern isn’t something that is applied to the surface afterwards – it is created through the material itself by layering, compressing, slicing and rebuilding different coloured clays,” he said. “There is always this balance between control and chance, which is something I love about the process.”

“Working with the Harlequin team and looking at those surfaces and identifying elements within them that could become a wallpaper or a fabric was fascinating,” he continued.

“We were able to isolate gestures, enlarge details and play with scale in ways I wouldn’t necessarily have considered. Some tiny detail from a ceramic piece can suddenly become this huge, immersive pattern across a wall.”

Holland has a personal connection to each of the four fabrics developed for the collection – Southborough, Elsworthy, Great Hey and Blenets Check Mini – and each was named after one of his and his partner’s former homes.

“We created a really autobiographical narrative by naming the patterns and pieces in the collection after homes that my husband and I have lived in through our lives,” he said.

While the patterning on the fabrics, which ranges from checkerboard in Blenets Check Mini to moiré-style in Elsworthy and chevrons in Southborough, was informed by ceramics, so too were the colours selected.

Pastel tones of chocolate and moss were informed by unglazed pottery, while Holland looked to glazed earthenware for the collection’s bolder colours.

“We were able to split the palette into more subdued, almost pastel tones, taking our lead from our unglazed ceramics, and then a bolder level of colour where we used our glazed pieces as the reference,” explained Holland.

“It was really important to me that, even though we were translating the work into completely different materials and applications, everything still felt very rooted in the studio and recognisably ours.”

Although the fabrics and wallpapers in the collection each have a distinct aesthetic and feel, Holland believes the pieces form a coherent collection because they come from a shared creative thought process.

“They share a common DNA because ultimately they all come back to the same source material, which is the ceramics,” he said.

“Within my ceramic work there has always been a contrast between very precise pattern and much looser, more organic pattern. Some pieces can be incredibly controlled and almost mathematical, while others are much more fluid. I didn’t want to lose that contrast when translating the work into print,” he continued.

“What brings everything together is colour, movement and the sense that everything has been touched by hand. Even when the patterns are quite different, there is a shared irregularity and energy to them. Nothing feels too perfect or overly digital, and that was really important to me.”

Holland hopes designers will use the collection’s fabrics in a wide variety of interiors, working out how to combine and layer pieces to create unique and interesting spaces.

“I don’t think there should be too many rules around how it is used,” he said. “One of the things we really wanted was for the collection to have enough cohesion that you could layer different elements together without everything having to match perfectly.”

“The colour stories run throughout the collection, so you can pick up a tone from one of the more expressive wallpapers and echo it through a fabric or a quieter pattern elsewhere in the room,” continued Holland. “I think interiors are much more interesting when there is that kind of tension.”

Overall, Holland hopes people will enjoy using the fabrics and wallpapers and enjoy the spaces that are created.

“Ultimately, I want people to have fun with it,” he said. “I like interiors that feel collected and personal rather than overly prescribed.”

“Hopefully the collection gives designers and customers the tools to create spaces that have personality, warmth and a real sense of individuality,” he continued.

The collection is the result of a deep collaboration between Holland and Harlequin, which has resulted in its success.

“It was a very genuine back-and-forth process,” said Holland. “I didn’t want to simply hand over some ceramic patterns and say, ‘turn these into wallpaper’.”

“The interesting part was bringing together what we know about ceramics and pattern at Henry Holland Studio with Harlequin’s incredible knowledge of textiles, wallpaper, colour and interiors,” he continued.

“We started with the ceramics and the archive of patterns and colour combinations we have developed at the studio, and from there the Harlequin team began exploring scale, repeats, textures and different interpretations. We would respond to those, push certain things further, pull other things back and keep refining the palette.”

Holland believes this close collaboration is key to the collection’s success.

“I think the best collaborations happen when both sides bring something to the project that the other couldn’t necessarily achieve alone,” he said.

“There are things in this collection that feel Henry Holland Studio completely, but they have been transformed through Harlequin’s expertise into something entirely new. That’s what made the whole process so rewarding.”

A year ago, a lot of people couldn't quite believe it when Canva made Affinity free. Suddenly, the three paid-for apps obtained through the acquisition of Serif were rolled into a single piece of creative software covering everything from photo editing to vector art and desktop publishing, simultaneously serving as a free Photoshop alternative, InDesign alt and Illustrator alt.

There had to be a catch, and one of the suspicions was that the new Affinity would be unlikely to get regular upgrades or improvements. One year on, Canva seems to be defying those predictions. It added new raw photo editing capabilities last month, with more colour, sharpening and detail adjustments. Today, it's completed things by adding one major element that was still missing for many creatives' workflows: a dedicated Affinity for iPad.

The individual Affinity apps (Affinity Photo 2, Designer 2, Publisher 2) were previously available for iPad before last year's launch of the unified free Affinity for desktop. Users who had bought them could continue using the apps, but they didn't support the new .af file format.

The new single-app Affinity for iPad brings the bulk of the combined desktop software to Apple tablets but designed specifically for a touch-first interface. It also takes advantage of Apple Pencil capabilities like pressure and tilt for sketching or for masking images, as well as Apple Pencil Pro's barrel roll, squeeze and hover features.

The app features Sketch Studio for freehand drawing and sketch-to-vector workflows, and several iPad-first features like a Mask Tool and Sketch to Shapes.

Like on the desktop app, Affinity for iPad uses the same .af file format across sketch, vector, photo and layout processes to make cross-media workflows easier. Non-destructive edits render in real time and there's no need for assets to be exported, converted or remade.

For sketching, there's a brush library with controls to shape each brush, while sketches stay live in the file to build on, rather than trace again. The iPad app also includes Affinity's raw image editing capabilities and the ability to create print-ready multi-page documents.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

AI tools, including Generative Expand, upscaling, denoising, and Decompose Layer to split a flat image into editable layers, are available with a subscription via Canva AI Studio.

An increasing range of major software is now available in the form of dedicated iPad apps, from Adobe's main apps like Photoshop, Illustrator and Premiere to DaVinci Resolve for video editing and Maxon's ZBrush for 3D sculpting. This means the powerful iPad Pro can now be used to its full potential for creative work, allowing more mobile workflows, either for working remotely or simply allowing creatives to take time away from the desk to work in another place before coming back to pick things up on desktop.

Affinity for iPad is is free for individual users and available to download from the iPad App Store now. If you don't already have one, you'll need to create a free Canva account to use the app. A premium Canva subscription is required for AI tools.

#9092. Italy Looks to Join Its European Counterparts With Restitution Legislation

Italy is joining other European countries, including Germany, Austria, France, the Netherlands, the UK, and Switzerland, in establishing its own restitution laws. The legislation was introduced by a lawmaker from Brothers of Italy, the right-wing populist political party in Italy that is currently the country’s ruling party, led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

The Art Newspaper reports that if the bill is considered, a five-member committee will be established by government officials, giving the committee the task of examining the provenance of works between 1933 and 1945 that were confiscated, looted, or sold under duress. Related Articles Italian Carabinieri Are Training Professionals Across Africa to Stop Antiquities Trafficking Bavarian State Painting Collections in Munich Returns Painting to Great-Grandson of Jewish Collector Who Fled Germany in 1938

“Introducing this bill does not merely mean finally bringing Italy into line with the highest international standards … but [it] means, first and foremost, fulfilling a historic duty,” Federico Mollicone, member of the chamber of deputies of Italy and president of the culture commission in Italy’s lower house of parliament, told TAN.

Mollicone introduced the bill in March and said that this law is not “merely talking about property claims” but a larger conversation to be had around “restoring human dignity, memory and the fundamental principles of our constitution.”

Compared to other European countries, Italy has lacked pace in developing restitution protocols for dispossessed Jews. “Italy is obviously a central country in the world of art … and yet on this issue of the Holocaust restitution, it had barely scratched the surface in addressing it,” Gideon Taylor, the president of World Jewish Restitution Organisation, told TAN. France’s restitution and compensation committee was created in 1999, and in 2000, the UK established its Spoliation Advisory Panel, an advisory body that works on cultural property looted during the Nazi era.

However, passing such legislation in Italy is bound to be a challenge, as works held in Italian museums are recognized as inalienable parts of the national heritage under the law. The bill that Mollicone has proposed argues that the final restitution decision would remove the work from public domain and the protections of Italy’s heritage code, potentially resulting in the works leaving the country. Mollicone said his goal is to “complete the parliamentary review and pass the bill in the coming months. We want to bring this historic reform to a successful conclusion within this legislative session.”

It's been a while since I saw an optical illusion good enough to share, but I couldn't resist this one, which is like a combination of two of our favourite ever optical illusions. I present: the spinning horse meets the blue and black or white and gold dress – and it's baffling the internet.

This is a real life video of a horse standing in a stable. And the horse is clearly black... except, it isn't. Apparently it's white. I absolutely cannot see this however many times I come back to it, but people in the comments have learned how the horse is actually in shadow, clicked off and back onto it, and then can see that it's white.

I'll share it below – can you see the horse as its real colour, or are you stuck in the same camp as me?

With 4,500 upvotes on Reddit, the r/opticalillusions subreddit is taken with this illusion.

"I can no longer see it as a black horse but at first it was as black as midnight. Now it's white and I cant make it go back," one amazed comment reads.

"It's the exact same effect as the White/Gold Blue/Black dress," explains another. "It's an image where the subject is in shadow but the background is in bright sunlight and our brain struggles to differentiate the two lighting conditions."

Other comments share tips on how to achieve the effect if you're struggling.

#9090. Miquel Navarro, Sculptor of Large-Scale, Pared-Down Cities and Valencia’s Beloved ‘Pink Panther,’ Dies at 81

Miquel Navarro, a sculptor known for his pared-down installation of cities that reflected on the promises of modernity in the latter-half of the 20th century, died on Sunday at 81 in Mislata, Spain, after a long illness, reports El País.

Navarro’s hometown of Mislata, just outside València, served as a never-ending source of inspiration for him throughout his career. “The city that inspired part of his imagery was also where he lived, worked, and developed much of his creative process. From his studio in the Morería neighborhood, the artist built a universal career without ever relinquishing his connection to the land where he grew up,” the Mislata City Council said in a statement announcing his death. Related Articles Vietnamese-American Photographer and Oberlin Professor Pipo Nguyen-duy Found Dead at 64 Tony Berlant, Artist Known for Cut Metal Collages, Dies at 85

Part of a generation of Spanish artists who came to prominence in the 1980s, Navarro would make his first “City” sculpture in 1973, two years before the Franco regime ended. “In the fifties, I would approach the city on a tram, and the encounter with it was fascinating,” he told El País in 2009 of his inspiration for the decades-long series.

Meant to be walked around and through, these installations feature first dozens and then hundreds of elements in various shapes, from cuboids and truncated pyramids representing rows of homes or the campuses of factories to soaring cylinders and columns, stand-ins for skyscrapers.

“Even my most schematic sculptures, without entirely abandoning the figurative, always bear the marks of man,” he once said of his “Cities.” The earliest of these would be comprised of dozens of pieces of clay, though he would later fabricate his “Cities” from metals like aluminum and iron.

While some portions of the installation show the rigid order of a city grid, other parts feature elements strewn about, toppled over—a metaphor for the parts of the urban environment that can’t be as easily organized.

“Navarro’s cities generate arenas for the confrontation of ideas. Throughout his career, he has continually proposed a revision of our notions of space, construction, place, and of our own bodies as a singular measure of the human and the city,” reads an exhibition description for the Guggenheim Museum’s 2004 display of his Wall City (1995–2000), which had recently been acquired by the Guggenheim Bilbao.

A few years later, Navarro would offer another reading to his sculptures: “Eroticism is a very important part of my work,” Navarro told El Mundo in a 2009 interview. “On the one hand, it is represented by the totem pole, which is not only a human, phallic element, but a symbol of solitude and power, as is the case with skyscrapers.”

Calling him a “beloved son of Mistlata,” the Mislata City Council declared three days of official mourning from November 1–3, describing him as “one of the great figures of contemporary Spanish art, whose work has achieved international recognition and whose name will forever remain linked to the history, identity and collective memory of his hometown.”

Miquel Narravo was born on September 29, 1945, in Mislata. In 1964, he first took up painting and drawing before devoting himself exclusively to sculpture in 1974, according to a chronology produced by the Guggenheim Bilbao. He studied fine arts at the Escuela Superior de Bellas Artes de San Carlos in Valencia before dropping out in 1968, the year he participated in a group exhibition, “Nuestro yo,” at Círculo Universitario de Valencia.

In 1972, the year of his first solo show, Navarro begins working in sculpture before debuting his first “City” sculpture, La ciutat (1973–74), the following year at the Galería Val i 30 in Valencia.

Navarro would gain international attention for his inclusion in the 1980 exhibition “New Images from Spain” at the Guggenheim Museum in New York. In 1986, he would represent Spain at the Venice Biennale, alongside other artists of his generation, Ferran García Sevilla, José María Sicilia, and Cristina Iglesias. That same year, he won the Premio Nacional de Artes Plásticas (National Award for Plastic Arts), Spain’s top award for artists, given out by the Ministry of Culture. A 1989 exhibition at the Reina Sofía would see his 55-foot sculpture Minerva paranoica (Paranoid Minerva) installed in Madrid’s Palacio de Cristal.

The mid-1980s would also see Navarro engage in public sculpture, with the installation of his towering 75-foot painted-iron water fountain Fuente Pública (Public Fountain, 1986) in Valencia, meant to commemorate “the transfer of water from the Júcar River to Valencia,” per the Guggenheim Bilbao. The now-iconic sculpture would lovingly be called by its citizens La Pantera Rosa (The Pink Panther), for the pinkish hue it would get over the years and its resemblance to the cartoon character.

He would go on to make several other sculptures for cities across Spain and abroad. For Barcelona, he created Fraternitat (Fraternity, 1992), and for his hometown he would make three public works: Cabeza con luna menguante (Head with Waning Moon, 2001), L’Almassil (2010), and Caminante (Walker, 2022).

His love for Mislata and Valencia would see him donate hundreds of works for the public to enjoy. In 2005, he gave 530 works to the Institut Valencià d’Art Modern (IVAM). Then, in 2020, he created the Fundació Miquel Navarro to preserve his legacy, seeding it with a donation of over 400 works, including several “Cities” installations. Sited in his longtime studio, a 10,800-square-foot former warehouse that he moved into in the 1980s, the foundation opened to the public this past June the artist’s Casa-Taller (House-Workshop) to show some of the donated works.

“Today Mislata has bid farewell not only to a universal artist, but also to a generous and humble friend, a person deeply connected to this city,” Mislata mayor Carlos F. Bielsa said in a statement. “His House-Studio will always be the legacy and the greatest treasure we have to preserve and cherish his memory.
